title: Buy back MOL's stake and restore Croatian ownership of the INA oil company
description: On 24 December 2016, after an UNCITRAL arbitral tribunal in Geneva rejected Croatia's claims against the Hungarian group MOL, Plenković announced that the government had decided to regain ownership of INA by buying MOL's entire stake, under a model that would 'not increase Croatia's public debt'. He said he had repeated the aim 'both during the election campaign and after assuming the office of Prime Minister'.
reasoning: The government formed a council for the buy-back in January 2017 and selected investment advisers in 2018, but in December 2018 Plenković said that failing to agree on a price could become 'an insurmountable problem'. In late December 2021, after the Supreme Court upheld the bribery conviction of former prime minister Ivo Sanader in the INA–MOL case, Plenković said the government was suspending the buy-out while it sought the annulment of the arbitration award (BBJ, citing MTI). Dnevnik Nova TV's review of his ten years in office (October 2026) states that he did not fulfil the promise to return INA to state ownership.
key_evidence: 24 December 2016: government announces decision to buy MOL's entire stake in INA (vlada.gov.hr)
January 2017: council for negotiations with MOL formed; April 2018: consortium of Morgan Stanley, Intesa Sanpaolo and PBZ chosen as adviser, contract not signed by December 2018 (vlada.gov.hr)
4 December 2018: Plenković says lack of agreement on price may become 'insurmountable'
December 2021: buy-out effort suspended pending a challenge to the UNCITRAL award (BBJ/MTI)
October 2026: Dnevnik Nova TV lists the INA pledge as unfulfilled after ten years

title: Ratify the Council of Europe's Istanbul Convention on violence against women
description: In November 2016 Plenković said the government would ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. In 2018 he presented it as 'primarily a convention that should promote national mechanisms for protection against violence against women and domestic violence', acknowledging 'the sensitivity of some social groups'.
reasoning: Parliament adopted the ratification act on 13 April 2018 (Narodne novine – International Treaties 3/2018). The act attaches an interpretative declaration stating that Croatia considers the Convention does not oblige it to introduce 'gender ideology' into its legal and educational systems or to change the constitutional definition of marriage. The commitment was delivered in his first term, with that declaration added.
key_evidence: Plenković recalled in 2018 that he had said in November 2016 that the government would ratify the convention (vlada.gov.hr)
13 April 2018: Sabor adopts the ratification act, published in NN-MU 3/2018 on 16 May 2018
The act includes an interpretative declaration on 'gender ideology' and the constitutional definition of marriage

title: Build the LNG terminal on the island of Krk
description: Plenković defended the floating LNG terminal on Krk against local protests and opposition criticism in 2018, calling it a strategic investment project that would put Croatia 'in an adequate place on the energy map of Europe' and noting EU funding of more than EUR 100 million.
reasoning: The terminal and the Omišalj–Zlobin connecting pipeline were officially inaugurated by Plenković on 29 January 2021, according to the European Commission's executive agency CINEA. The floating storage and regasification unit has a maximum send-out capacity of 2.6 billion cubic metres a year and received EUR 124 million from the Connecting Europe Facility. The project was completed as committed.
key_evidence: 2018: Plenković says the government is going ahead with the Krk LNG terminal despite protests (vlada.gov.hr)
29 January 2021: terminal and pipeline inaugurated by Plenković (CINEA)
Capacity 2.6 bcm/year; EUR 124 million EU CEF funding

title: Raise the statutory retirement age to 67 (2018 pension reform)
description: The pension reform drawn up by Plenković's first government and adopted by parliament on 7 December 2018 set the right to an old-age pension at 67 years of age and 15 years of contributions from 1 January 2033, with the age rising gradually from 2028, and tightened early retirement.
reasoning: In 2019 the trade-union initiative '67 je previše' ('67 is too much') collected about 700,000 signatures for a referendum against the reform, and Plenković announced that the government would present amendments that 'respect the will of citizens' (Emerging Europe). Parliament adopted those amendments on 18 October 2019 (NN 102/2019), restoring the right to an old-age pension at 65 years of age and 15 years of contributions from 1 January 2020. The central element of the reform was reversed less than a year after adoption.
key_evidence: NN 115/2018 (adopted 7 December 2018): retirement at 67 from 1 January 2033
2019: union referendum initiative '67 je previše' collects about 700,000 signatures
NN 102/2019 (adopted 18 October 2019): retirement at 65 with 15 years of contributions, in force from 1 January 2020

title: Adopt the euro on 1 January 2023
description: In September 2021 Plenković said he was confident Croatia would be ready to enter the euro area on 1 January 2023 and would fulfil in time 'all the commitments we undertook by entering the Exchange Rate Mechanism'. He said no referendum was needed, as Croatia had accepted the obligation to adopt the euro when it voted to join the EU.
reasoning: Parliament adopted the Act on the Introduction of the Euro as the Official Currency on 13 May 2022 (NN 57/2022), and Croatia joined the euro area on 1 January 2023, as the government's investment agency records. The target date set by Plenković was met.
key_evidence: 13 September 2021: Plenković confident of joining the euro area on 1 January 2023 (vlada.gov.hr)
13 May 2022: Euro Introduction Act adopted (NN 57/2022)
1 January 2023: Croatia adopts the euro

title: Join the Schengen area together with the euro area
description: After the European Council backed Croatia's euro-area entry in June 2022, Plenković said the next step was Schengen accession, with a decision expected in the autumn, and that on 1 January 2023 Croatia would enter the euro area and the Schengen area simultaneously.
reasoning: Croatia joined the Schengen area on 1 January 2023, the same day as the euro area, according to the government's investment agency. Schengen membership had been a long-standing goal of his governments; the specific timing he announced in June 2022 was achieved.
key_evidence: 24 June 2022: Plenković says Croatia would enter the euro area and Schengen on 1 January 2023 (vlada.gov.hr)
1 January 2023: Croatia joins the Schengen area and the euro area

title: Complete OECD accession by the end of 2025 and become a member in 2026
description: At the OECD Council in Paris on 30 October 2023 Plenković called OECD membership Croatia's 'last strategic foreign-policy goal' and said the accession process should be completed by the end of 2025, 'with the ambition that formal membership be realised in 2026'.
reasoning: Croatia applied in January 2017, the OECD opened accession talks in January 2022 and reviews in 25 committees and 26 sub-committees began in November 2022. According to the government's OECD page, Croatia is 'in the final phase' of accession, with the conditions met in 21 of the 25 committees and in all 26 sub-committees (status September 2026). The end-2025 deadline was missed and, as of October 2026, Croatia is not yet a member.
key_evidence: 25 January 2017: letter of intent; 25 January 2022: OECD Council opens talks; 10 June 2022: accession roadmap
30 October 2023: Plenković sets end-2025 for completion and 2026 for membership
Second OECD Economic Survey presented on 30 January 2026
September 2026: 21 of 25 committees and all 26 sub-committees closed (vlada.gov.hr)

title: Raise the average net wage to EUR 1,600 by 2028
description: The programme of Plenković's third government (2024–2028), published by the Sabor on 16 May 2024, sets the goals that the average net wage reach EUR 1,600, that 125,000 jobs be created and that the employment rate reach 75 percent.
reasoning: According to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, the average monthly net wage paid in legal entities was EUR 1,540 in July 2026, 7.2 percent higher in nominal terms and 3.2 percent higher in real terms than a year earlier; the median net wage was EUR 1,346. The target is close but not yet reached, with about a year and a half of the term remaining.
key_evidence: Government programme 2024–2028: average net wage EUR 1,600, 125,000 new jobs, 75% employment rate (tportal)
DZS: average net wage EUR 1,540 in July 2026 (+7.2% nominal year on year); median EUR 1,346

title: Raise the average pension to at least EUR 750 by the end of the term (later EUR 800)
description: The 2024–2028 government programme states that by the end of the term the average pension should be at least EUR 750. On 1 October 2025 Plenković raised the goal, saying the government's aim was an average 'total' pension (including special categories and the annual pension supplement) of EUR 800 by the end of the term.
reasoning: On 21 October 2026 Plenković told the cabinet that the total average pension was 'about EUR 780' and announced that the annual pension supplement would rise to an average of EUR 208, bringing the government closer to its EUR 800 target. The figures depend on the definition used: the government counts the 'total' average including special schemes and the supplement, while pensioners' representatives argue that pensions lag behind wages (tportal, July 2026). Progress is documented, but the raised target has not yet been met; confidence is moderate because of the differing measures.
key_evidence: Programme 2024–2028: average pension at least EUR 750 by the end of the term
1 October 2025: Plenković sets a EUR 800 target for the average total pension; says it would exceed EUR 704 at the end of 2025
21 October 2026: Plenković says the total average pension is about EUR 780; annual supplement raised to an average EUR 208 (vlada.gov.hr)
July 2026: the pensioners' party BUZ says pensions are about EUR 170 short of a promised 60% of the average wage (tportal)

title: Reintroduce compulsory basic military training from 2026
description: In 2025 the government sent parliament amendments to the Defence Act and the Armed Forces Service Act reintroducing compulsory basic military training (temeljno vojno osposobljavanje), suspended since 2008. Plenković said that with 'well-calibrated' training 'we create the preconditions for young generations to acquire skills that 17 or 18 generations have not acquired'; the two-month training was to start in January 2026.
reasoning: Parliament passed the amendments on 24 October 2025. The Ministry of Defence sent the first medical-examination invitations on 29 December 2025; the first intake of 800 conscripts reported for training in March 2026, a second intake of 900 began in May 2026 and the third intake was raised to 1,000 in August 2026, with a monthly pay of about EUR 1,100 net. The start slipped from January to March 2026, but the measure is in force and operating.
key_evidence: Government bill: two-month training in Knin, Slunj and Požega, up to 4,000 conscripts a year, alternative civilian service for conscientious objectors (Informator)
24 October 2025: Sabor passes the amendments (MORH)
March 2026: 800 conscripts of the first intake report; May 2026: 900 in the second intake; August 2026: third intake raised to 1,000 (MORH)
